title: Strongly History-Independent Storage Allocation: New Upper and Lower Bounds
abstract: A data structure is said to be \emph{strongly history independent} if its state is fully determined by its current set of elements (and random bits). One of the most basic questions that strongly history-independent algorithms face is storage allocation: given a set $S$ of up to $(1 - \epsilon)n + 1$ elements, assign them to distinct positions in an array of size $n$. If we ask that the allocation be strongly history independent, then what is the optimal asymptotic cost of performing an insertion or deletion? On the upper-bound side, Berger et al. (ICALP '22)~showed how to achieve expected cost $O(1 + \log \epsilon^{-1})$. In this paper, we offer a nearly matching lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}(\log \epsilon^{-1})$. As corollaries, we get nearly tight lower bounds for strongly history-independent hashing (STOC '01, FOCS '07, ICALP '08) and for the so-called memoryless worker-task assignment problem (SSS '17, ICALP '20, ICALP '22). Next we consider the problem of partitioning an array of size $n$ among many items of different sizes (and whose cumulative sizes are at most $(1 - \epsilon)n + 1$). In STOC '01, Naor and Teague gave a \emph{weakly} history-independent solution to this problem with logarithmic overhead (and with $\epsilon = 1/2$); they posed as an open question whether one could hope to do better. We give a new construction that achieves $O(1)$ expected overhead, also for $\epsilon = 1/2$, and that is \emph{strongly} history independent. Generalizing to $\epsilon < 1/2$, our solution achieves expected overhead $O(1 + \log \epsilon^{-1})$ for insertion/deletions of objects whose sizes are at most $O(\epsilon^4 n)$.

A data structure ALG is said to be strongly history independent (or uniquely representable) if its state is fully determined

depend on the order in which elements were inserted, or on the

Our ﬁrst result: a nearly tight lower bound. We establish a
nearly tight lower bound for the Stateless Allocation problem,

Our lower bound applies to any  ≥ 1/n and to any universe

This Paper: New Upper and Lower Bounds
The main results of this paper are twofold. First, we give
a nearly tight lower bound of Ω̃(log −1 ) on the expected
overhead incurred by any Stateless Allocation algorithm—
as an immediate consequence, we also get nearly tight lower
bounds for closely related problems in hashing [1], [17], [20],
[21], [34] and distributed computing [16], [37], [38]. Second,
we present an algorithm with expected overhead O(−1 ) for
the Variable-Size Stateless Allocation Problem—this is the
ﬁrst algorithm to achieve an overhead that is a function of
 rather than n [34]. Both of these results resolve wellestablished open problems, the latter of which was proposed
more than two decades ago in the seminal paper on strong
history independence by Naor and Teague [34].
In the rest of the section, we discuss these results in more
detail, along with the related prior work.

Variations of the problem. It is worth making explicit the
differences between the version of the Variable-Size Stateless Allocation Problem studied here (i.e., strongly history
independent) and the one studied in prior work [34] (i.e.,
weakly history independent). Because the results in [34] are
for the weakly history-independent version of the problem,
they need not require that allocations are associated with
unique names (i.e., keys): the distribution of possible states can
be determined by the (multi-)set of item sizes that are currently
present. If one wishes to discuss strong history independence,
then one must require that items have names (so that the state
can be a function of the items that are present). However,
one can also apply our results directly to the setting of [34]
(weak history independence without names) by generating
(artiﬁcial) random item names whenever allocations occur.
Thus our model can be viewed as encapsulating both the
weakly history-independent setting and the strongly historyindependent setting each in their simplest possible forms.
It is also worth commenting on the distinctions between
the version of the Fixed-Size Stateless Allocation Problem
studied here (which is adapted from [34]) and the model
independently introduced in [16], [37], [38]. These works
study the problem of assigning a multi-set of w tasks T ⊆ [t] to
workers 1, 2, . . . , w in a strongly history-independent fashion.
If T is a set (rather than a multi-set), then their problem is
exactly equivalent to ours (tasks are items, and workers are
array slots). As noted in [16], however, as long as t ≥ poly w,
the assumption that T is a (non-multi) set is without loss of
generality, up to increasing the universe size w by a polynomial factor. With this reduction in place, the two problems
become equivalent.

V. O PEN Q UESTIONS
We conclude the paper with several open questions:
1) In the variable-size case, our O(1 + log −1 )-overhead
result represents a new state-of-the-art even for nonhistory-independent solutions. However, this result applies only to the setting where objects are guaranteed to
be relatively small (size less than 4 n) compared to the
size of memory. We conjecture that, if larger objects are
allowed, then the folklore bound of O(−1 ) overhead
should be optimal. A hard case would seem to be the
one where the are Θ(−1 ) objects with real-valued sizes
between 1 and 2. Can one, in this case, do anything
asymptotically better than simply rebuilding the entire
array on each insertion/deletion?
2) In the variable-size case, it remains an open question
whether our overhead of O(1 + log −1 ) is optimal
for weakly history-independent solutions. Although our
result represents a signiﬁcant improvement to the best
known upper bound for this case [34], there is still no
nontrivial lower bound known.
3) In the ﬁxed-size case, Berger et al. [16] show that
it is possible to achieve deterministic worst-case cost
O(log2 n). This is the only instance we are aware
of where a nontrivial guarantee can be offered by a
data structure that is both strongly history independent
and deterministic. Whether their bound is optimal (or
whether it can be reduced to, e.g., Õ(log n)) remains an
intriguing open question.
